Introduction

Hello, I'm Shane

I'm a game engineer who works on gameplay systems and applied generative AI. I made Fuzzle and the Shifting Woods to explore one question in a small, finished game: how do you let generated content into gameplay and keep the design in charge?

Three things in Fuzzle are generated while you play: the levels, the characters' lines, and the music. Each one has a deterministic layer around it. A level only ships if a checker proves it can be finished. A character's line only reaches the player if it matches the game's real state and stays in character. When a generator fails, the game falls back to something it knows is correct.

This page covers the story and art first, then each generated system, the tools I use to tune and debug them, and the technology underneath. The whole game runs in a web browser with a keyboard or a gamepad.

The story

Fuzzle's family has been stolen

The story is told in storybook panels between levels, and every panel is drawn live in code. These are the panels as they appear in the game, with their real text.

  1. 1In the soft green hills of Puffhollow lived Fuzzle and the fluffiest family you ever saw.

  2. 2Then one stormy night, the warlock Oink swept into Puffhollow, tusks gleaming and cloak swirling.

  3. 3He locked Fuzzle's brother and sisters in cages and hid them in the Mossy Woods, the Crystal Caves, and the Cloud Tops. Mama, Papa, and baby Pip he kept in his tower. Then he cursed the land so it shifts every time someone falls.

  4. 4But the curse could not hide the three Heart Crystals. Gather them, little Fuzzle, free your family, and break Oink's spell.

  5. 5The Heart of the Woods! Oink's curse on the Mossy Woods breaks, and Ember is free! Next stop: the Crystal Caves.

  6. 6Warlock Oink: "So the little fluffball came for its family. How adorable. Your shiny pebbles are no match for MY magic!"

  7. 7With the power of all three Heart Crystals, Fuzzle broke the spell. The great warlock Oink shrank into a very small, very grumpy piglet.

  8. 8The curse lifted, the lands bloomed again, and the whole family went home to Puffhollow together.

The story sets the rules of a run. Each of the three lands ends with a caged sibling and a Heart Crystal. In Oink's Tower, each crystal-powered hit on Oink frees baby Pip, then Mama Plum, then Papa Clover, and freed family members follow Fuzzle for the rest of the run. Falling is part of the story too: Oink's curse reshapes the land each time Fuzzle falls, which is why the levels regrow.

Characters and art

Drawn in code, readable at a glance

Every character is drawn with the Canvas 2D API at runtime, with no sprite sheets. The family shares one fluffy silhouette with its own colors and topper for each member, so a freed sibling is easy to pick out even when small and moving. Their faces change with mood: happy, scared, sad, brave or poofed.

The world

Three cursed lands and a tower

Generative AI

Generated while you play, checked by the game

Three parts of Fuzzle are generated at runtime. The characters' dialogue is the generative AI system, built around a model-ready generator. The levels and the music are procedural generation. All three follow the same rule: a generator proposes, and deterministic game logic decides what the player gets.

1 · Character dialogue with a guard layer

Old Hoot, Croaksworth and Dot all speak through one pipeline. What they say depends on the run: how many seeds are left and in which direction, which hazards this level has, who in the family is free, what is in stock, and what keeps poofing Fuzzle. Players can also type anything to them.

  1. 1FactsThe game builds a snapshot of everything this character may know right now. Nothing outside it can be stated as fact.
  2. 2DraftThe generator returns JSON: the line, plus structured claims, shop offers or a quest.
  3. 3GuardDeterministic checks compare the draft with the facts. Small problems are fixed in place, such as a price clamped into range.
  4. 4RetryIf anything would mislead the player, the generator gets one retry with the problems listed.
  5. 5FallbackIf the retry fails or the generator is down, the character says a written line built from the same facts.
Every line in the game is labeled with how it got there: Generated · checked Generated · adjusted by the guard Generated · fixed on retry Written line · draft blocked
CheckWhat the guard catches
FactsWrong seed counts, directions that point at nothing, hazards this level doesn't have, a family member called caged when they are already free.
EconomyItems that aren't in stock, prices outside each item's floor and cap, a line that quotes a price the shop board doesn't show.
QuestsItems the level can't place, rewards outside 2 to 5 seeds, a quest line that never says what to look for.
CharacterTalk of AI, prompts, phones or the internet, and invented names or places.
SafetyUnkind words in either direction. Typed messages that try to rewrite the character's rules are flagged so the character answers in-world.
FormatReplies that aren't valid JSON or have no line, and lines longer than 220 characters.
Draft
Hoo! Three seeds left. The nearest is a short walk to the north-west. And watch out for the bees. Beware the lava pits.
Guard
facts: Warned about lava, which this level doesn't have.
Retry
Hoo! Three seeds left. The nearest is a short walk to the north-west. Mind the ponds. The portal sleeps to the north.
Shown
Generated · fixed on retry

All checks passed on the retry. Old Hoot's claims (3 seeds, nearest to the north-west, ponds on this level) all match the facts.

Personality against balance

Croaksworth has a generosity setting. A generous frog cuts his prices when Fuzzle has been poofed a lot in this land, and a stingy one marks them up. Each item has a floor at 60% and a cap at 125% of its base price, and only the guard enforces them. Personality can move prices, but it can't break the economy.

When you buy, the game charges the verified price on the shop board, never a number taken from the text. Croaksworth also remembers your run, and the guard checks that memory too: if he says the bees got you three times, it has to be three.

Typed messages are cleaned and capped at 140 characters before the generator sees them. Unkind messages skip the generator and get a written reply. The world pauses while a conversation is open, so the facts can't change while a line is being written.

What writes the lines today

This build ships with a built-in offline generator. It writes each line from the facts using authored patterns and each character's personality rules, so the game runs anywhere with no network and no cost. The generator sits behind one swappable generate() function, and connecting a hosted language model through it is the next milestone. The facts, guard, fallbacks and debug log stay the same, which is the point of the design.

0 of 100drafts with planted mistakes reached the player. 96 were fixed on retry and 4 had a price pulled back into range.
36 of 36clean drafts passed every check on the first try, across all three characters.

2 · Levels that regrow when you fall

Each level grows from a seed made of the run, the land, the level and the attempt number. When Fuzzle falls, the attempt number goes up and the level regrows into a new layout, so players learn the land instead of memorizing a map. The daily run uses the date as its seed, so everyone plays the same lands that day.

A level is a grid of chambers, 8 by 6 tiles each, filled from hand-made templates such as meadow, thicket, lanes and pond, and joined by a random spanning tree of doorways. Seeds, hazards and critters are placed by rule. A breadth-first search then proves that every seed and the portal can be reached from the start. A layout that fails is thrown away and regrown, up to 30 times, and as a last resort the generator carves a path.

Level 1-2 of one run, after Fuzzle falls twice: Hedge Bush Rock Brambles Thorn trap Pond Route the checker proved

3 · Music made in code

The soundtrack is one original 16-bar theme played by Web Audio synthesizers, so the game ships with no audio files. Each place gets its own arrangement of the same melody. Notes are scheduled slightly ahead on the audio clock so the beat stays steady when frames drop, and the music gets quieter during conversations and pauses.

Tools

Built-in tools for tuning and debugging

Press T in the game to open the developer panel. It's built for the questions that come up when generated content and game rules meet: what did the generator write, what did the game change, and why.

  • AI dialogue logEach draft, every check that fired, the retry, the final line and how long it took. It shows where generated content ends and game logic takes over.
  • Plant mistakesSlips wrong prices, wrong directions, invented names and out-of-world words into drafts at a chosen rate, to test the guard on demand.
  • Croaksworth's generosityA live personality slider for testing character against balance.
  • Level generatorThe seed, attempt, rejected layouts and templates for the current level, plus a Regrow button, the checker's route overlay and a jump to any level.
  • Feel tuningLive sliders for top speed, acceleration, stopping power, dash speed and dash cooldown.
Technology

A small stack with no assets

JavaScript
Plain JavaScript in 16 small modules plus one HTML page. No frameworks, libraries or build step.
Canvas 2D
Every character, tile, effect and story panel is drawn at runtime, with depth sorting and light masks for dark areas.
Web Audio API
Synthesized music and sound effects, scheduled on the audio clock.
Game loop
A fixed 120 Hz simulation step, so movement and physics feel the same at any frame rate.
Seeded randomness
A small seeded generator (mulberry32), so any level can be rebuilt exactly from its seed.
Input and saves
Keyboard and gamepad. Settings and best runs are saved in the browser.
Automated tests
During development, Playwright scripts played the game in headless Chromium to check level solvability, the boss fight, story flow, NPC placement and the dialogue guard.
Hosting
GitHub Pages. The game is static files, so it loads anywhere with no server.
Model-ready dialogue
One generate() contract for any generator, with the guard, fallbacks and log kept outside it.
Under the hood

How the JavaScript and the AI layer fit together

One frame of Fuzzle

  1. Read input. Keyboard and gamepad are polled once per display frame.
  2. Simulate in fixed steps. Movement, dashes, critters, Oink's attacks, hazards and pickups advance in steps of 1/120 of a second. A slow frame runs more steps, so the game plays the same at any frame rate. While a character is talking, the simulation holds still, so the facts behind a line stay true until it is shown.
  3. Queue the music. The next notes are scheduled on the audio clock about 0.18 seconds ahead, so the beat never depends on the frame rate.
  4. Draw. Ground tiles first, then everything that stands up, sorted by where its feet are, then the light mask for dark lands. The HUD and menus are HTML on top of the canvas.

Where generated content stops

The generator only decides the words. The game decides the facts: what is in stock, the price range of each item, where a quest item is placed, how many seeds a quest pays, and what Fuzzle is charged. A character can propose an offer or a quest, but it only takes effect after the guard checks it and the game applies it through its own rules.

This split is what makes the dialogue safe to swap. A hosted language model can replace the built-in generator without touching the guard, the shop, the quests or the debug log.

What's next

Connect a free hosted language model to the dialogue generator, behind the same guard. Add touch controls for phones. Add more lands and more for Fuzzle's friends to say.
